A chronological library of free English texts from the earliest Christian centuries onward. Links open on other sites. Category key: New Testament (link only); Saint / Church Father; Other early Christian; Disputed / noncanonical; Non-Christian witness.

AD 30–70 · Earliest years

Guiding questions
  • What happened after Jesus' death?
  • How did the apostles organize communities?
  • Where, how often, and how did Christians gather and worship?
  • How does the Eucharist relate historically to the Last Supper?
  • What did Peter, James, John, Paul and others do?
  • What happened as the apostles died?

Surviving narrative and letters for this generation are almost entirely canonical New Testament texts. External notices are brief and later copied. Silence is not evidence.

Evidence shows: New Testament texts that Christians preserved as scripture describe early Jerusalem and diaspora communities, a shared meal tradition, and named leaders; Josephus mentions James; Roman historians mention Christians in connection with Rome under Nero and Claudius.

Historians infer: Frequency of gatherings, exact local variety of meal practice, and day-to-day organization beyond what the texts happen to mention.

Still unknown: The full sequence of events after many apostles' deaths; most local community records; nearly all liturgical detail outside a few New Testament passages.

AD 70–150 · After the apostles

Guiding questions
  • How was apostolic teaching transmitted?
  • Who led afterward?
  • What about bishops, presbyters, and deacons?
  • What did ordinary Christian life, prayer, baptism, and Sunday worship look like?
  • How did churches communicate and stay united?
  • What did Christians believe before the later councils?

This is the densest surviving Christian letter-and-manual layer after the New Testament. Many texts traditionally linked to the apostles belong here.

Evidence shows: Letters from Rome, Antioch, and Smyrna; a church-order manual (Didache); an early martyr narrative for Polycarp; Pliny's provincial procedure under Trajan.

Historians infer: How universal any one local pattern was; exact authorship of anonymous works.

Still unknown: Most local archives; full biographies of most leaders; whether some manuals describe ideal or actual practice.

AD 150–325 · Developing Church

Guiding questions
  • How did the Mass and the sacraments take shape?
  • How was doctrine becoming defined?
  • What controversies arose?
  • What effects did persecution have?
  • What was the role of Rome and other churches?
  • How were authoritative writings determined?

From Justin's ritual descriptions through Irenaeus and the African and Latin writers to Eusebius and Nicaea, this period has the richest primary documentation for worship, conflict, and canon.

Evidence shows: Second-century apologies and church manuals; named controversies (Marcion, Gnostic teachers, Quartodeciman Pascha dispute, rebaptism); martyr acts; third-century unity and baptism debates; early fourth-century imperial shift in Lactantius and Eusebius; Nicaea creed and canons.

Historians infer: How typical any one city's liturgy was; motives in polemical sources.

Still unknown: Full texts of many opponents (often known only through critics); exact authorship of some church orders.

AD 325–1000 · After Constantine

Guiding questions
  • What changed after Constantine?
  • How did buildings, liturgy, vestments, art, and music develop?
  • Which councils clarified teaching?
  • How did monasticism grow?
  • How did East and West diverge?
  • Which early practices survived or changed?

Selective coverage. Favor documents that show practice (Egeria, Cyril's mystagogical lectures, Apostolic Constitutions 8, monastic rules) and the great Christological and creedal councils, plus II Nicaea on images.

Evidence shows: Imperial patronage narratives; catechetical and liturgical descriptions; monastic rules; conciliar definitions; pilgrim observation of Jerusalem rites.

Historians infer: How quickly local rites converged; how representative one pilgrim or one rule was.

Still unknown: Continuous musical notation for earliest chant; many ceremonial details before later Ordines.

AD 1000–present · Medieval Church onward

Guiding questions
  • How did the Mass reach recognizable forms?
  • How did spirituality, theology, and devotion develop?
  • Which modern Catholic traditions trace early, and which arose later?

Selective milestones: a short spine of Mass and doctrine documents alongside spiritual classics. These establish official teaching at dated moments; they do not by themselves prove day-to-day parish practice.

Evidence shows: Official teaching and rubrical policy at dated moments (councils, papal constitutions, spiritual classics).

Historians infer: Continuity claims with the earliest centuries are historical judgments, not automatic from the texts.

Still unknown: How every parish practiced day to day between these milestones.
